title: MSMS documentation
text:
Description
For a given set of spheres S and a probe radius rp, MSMS computes the reduced surface and the analytical model of the solvent excluded surface (SES). The SES can then be triangulated with a given vertex density.
The program runs in standalone mode or in server mode. In server mode, the only required option is the name of the socket used to communicate with the client application (-socket servicename or -sinetd).

title: MSMS documentation
text:
Options
Options may appear in any order and may be abbreviated. If an abbreviation matches several options, the first match is used.

Input and output

-if filename

The file from which the sphere set S is read. Each line holds the center (x, y, z) and the radius r of one sphere, in free format. Lines starting with # are comments and are skipped. This is the only required option in standalone mode.

-of filename

The files in which to store the triangulated solvent excluded surface. Two files are created, one for vertices and one for faces. For component 0 the files are filename.vert and filename.face. For other components the component number is inserted in the name; for component 3, for example, the files are filename_3.vert and filename_3.face.
Face file. Three header lines, then one triangle per line. The first header line holds a comment and the file name of the sphere set. The second describes the content of the third. The third gives the number of triangles, the number of spheres in the set, the triangulation density and the probe sphere radius. On each triangle line, the first three numbers are (1-based) vertex indices. The next field is 1 for a triangle in a toric reentrant face, 2 for a triangle in a spheric reentrant face and 3 for a triangle in a contact face. The last number is the (1-based) face number in the analytical description of the solvent excluded surface. Format: "%6d %6d %6d %2d %6d".
Vertex file. Three header lines (like those of the .face file), then one vertex per line: the coordinates (x, y, z) and the normal (nx, ny, nz), followed by the number of the face (in the analytical description of the surface) the vertex belongs to. Vertices of the analytical surface have 0 in that field, and vertices lying on edges of this surface have negative values. The next field is the (1-based) index of the closest sphere. The last field is 1 for vertices of toric reentrant faces (including vertices of the analytical surface), 2 for vertices inside reentrant faces and 3 for vertices inside contact faces. Format: "%9.3f %9.3f %9.3f %9.3f %9.3f %9.3f %7d %7d %2d".

-af filename

The file in which to store solvent excluded and solvent accessible surface areas. The areas in each surface component are listed for every atom.

-no_header

Do not write the 3-line header into the .face and .vert files (written by default).




Surface calculation

-probe_radius radius

Changes the probe sphere radius (default 1.5 Å). The value is not checked. MSMS fails to compute the triangulation template sphere for radii that are too small or too large; values from 0.5 to 10 should pose no problem.

-density density

Changes the triangulation density (default 1.0 vertex/Å2). The value is not checked. Typical values are 1.0 for large molecules (more than 1000 atoms) and 3.0 for smaller molecules.

-no_area

Turns off the surface area computation.

-surface <tses,ases>

Which surface to compute: tses for the triangulated solvent excluded surface, ases for the analytical solvent excluded surface. The default is the triangulated surface. This option is mainly used to skip triangulation, for instance when only surface areas are needed.

-noh

Skips atoms with radius 1.2.




Components

-free_vertices

Search for free vertices of the reduced surface (not done by default).

-all_components

Compute all components of the molecular surfaces (reduced and solvent excluded). By default only the external component is computed. With -of filename, a .vert and a .face file are written for each component.

-one_cavity #atoms at1 [at2] [at3]

Compute one specific component of the molecular surfaces by giving 1, 2 or 3 atoms the probe should initially touch: first the number of atoms, then their (0-based) indices.




Error recovery

-no_rest_on_pbr

Badly handled singular cases or numerical instability can make the triangulation fail. By default MSMS then restarts the computation, up to five times, after increasing the radius of the atoms causing the problem by 0.1 Å. This option prevents the restart when problems occur while triangulating spherical reentrant faces (which often points to singularities). The resulting triangulated surface will not be correct and may have holes (see also -no_rest).

-no_rest

Never restart the computation (see also -no_rest_on_pbr).




Server mode

-socket servicename

Starts MSMS in server mode, listening on the given Unix domain socket for clients requesting this service. When a client connects, MSMS receives the computation parameters and the spheres over the socket, and sends back the triangulated surface when the calculation is done. Values are not encoded in a portable way (such as XDR), so this works only on a limited set of architectures.

-sinetd

Puts MSMS in server mode when it is started by the internet daemon, so that MSMS starts whenever a client program requests it.

title: MSMS documentation
text:
Examples
Triangulate the solvent excluded surface of a set of spheres and save the triangulation in myset.vert and myset.face:
msms -if myset.xyzr -of myset
Compute the surface for a probe radius of 1.4 Å and triangulate it with a density of 3.0:
msms -if myset.xyzr -de 3.0 -prob 1.4 -of myset

title: MSMS documentation
text:
Known bugs

If all the vertices of a component of the reduced surface also belong to another component, MSMS fails to find this component. As a workaround, give the first face of that component explicitly with -one_cavity.
The genus of the reduced surface is sometimes wrong.
Singular edges forming full circles are not treated.
Normal vectors of singular vertices point arbitrarily to the center of one of the probes they belong to.
MSMS crashes or produces wrong results if a sphere of S lies entirely inside another sphere of S.

title: ADapt
text:
Warning



ADapt is not released yet. These pages describe a test version.


ADapt takes a PDB entry to receptor and ligand files ready for docking with the AutoDock suite, in a web browser.
A PDB file records a crystallographic experiment, not a molecule ready for docking. Preparing a receptor from it means making a series of choices: the asymmetric unit or a biological assembly, what to do with missing atoms and residues, which alternate location to keep, which cofactors, ligands, metals and waters to keep or remove. Most of these choices depend on where a fragment sits relative to the pocket you plan to dock into, so they are best made while looking at the structure.
ADapt reads a PDB file, or fetches it from the RCSB, and analyses it with ADFR’s own code, the same code as the PDB analyzer of AGFRgui. It builds every biological assembly the file defines, classifies every residue by what it is and what it needs, proposes the usual choices as defaults, and shows each chain as a tree linked to a 3D view.

title: AGFR documentation
text:
AutoGridFR (AGFR) generates target files: a single file that defines the binding site on a receptor targeted for docking. Target files make affinity maps easier to manage and support data provenance and reproducibility. They can be unzipped and the maps extracted for use with AutoDock4.
AGFR runs from the command line or through a graphical user interface (GUI). This page gives an overview of the GUI and a reference for its buttons. The tutorials walk through typical use cases step by step. Command-line examples are in the AutoDockFR tutorials.

title: AGFR documentation
text:
The graphical interface



The AGFR graphical user interface


Start the GUI with ADFRsuite-1.0/bin/agfrgui. The window title shows the program version and the names of the loaded receptor and ligand. If OpenMP is enabled, it also shows the number of available hardware threads.
The GUI has four areas:

Controls (left): stacked boxes of widgets for the steps of computing a target file for a receptor.
3D view (right): real-time visual feedback.
Toolbar (middle): buttons that change the representation in the 3D view.
Status bar (bottom): text about running computations or the next possible step, and status lights (red or green) that show whether the current docking box is valid.


Control panel

Receptor and ligand (top): load a receptor as a PDBQT file, or open an existing target file, which sets every widget the way the target file was generated. Optionally, load a crystallographic ligand to help position the docking box and/or choose the atom types for which to compute maps.
Docking box: buttons that size and position the box (the rectangular region over which affinity maps are computed) to enclose the entire receptor, the ligand (if loaded), a pocket (if pockets were found, see below), a set of receptor amino acids, or a box set by hand. Every button except the manual one computes the bounding box and adds the current padding on each side. The box must overlap the receptor, otherwise the BOX status light is red.
Flexible residues (“[0 flexible residue(s)]”): optionally make receptor side chains flexible, by typing a selection string or picking residues in a tree widget. The syntax is a chain ID, a colon and a comma-separated list of residues, for example A:LYS33,LYS89;B:ARG12. The box must cover the flexible residues, otherwise the FR light is red; a button enlarges the box to fix this. See the flexible side chains tutorial.
Covalent docking: optionally specify the 2 atoms that form the covalent bond between the receptor and the ligand, by picking them in the 3D view or typing their full names (for example A:CYS164:SG). A covalent ligand already present in the receptor is drawn with dashed lines and can be edited by adding or removing atoms. See the covalent docking tutorial.
Ligand binding pockets: a table of the pockets that AutoSite finds in the current box. Select fills to define the binding pocket. AutoSite 1.0 and 1.1 are both available; 1.1 is slower but describes pockets better, especially for larger ligands such as peptides.
Affinity maps: the atom types for which maps are computed. Computing maps for all AutoDock atom types is preferred, because the target file then works for any ligand. AGFR also computes water maps for hydrated docking automatically; their parameters are set here. You can also choose whether to add gradients to the maps, and set options for them.

Most buttons are enabled only once their prerequisites are met. For example, generate target file… is enabled only after a receptor is loaded, a box overlapping the receptor is defined, at least one pocket fill is selected, and that fill overlaps the box. The 4 status lights at the bottom right start red and turn green as conditions are met, which guides you through the workflow.
The maps are computed by an optimized, OpenMP-enabled version of AutoGrid4 bundled with AGFR.

title: Tutorial: maps for flexible receptor side chains
text:
In this scenario we have a receptor and a known ligand available in the PDBQT format and we define a docking box centered on the ligand.
We will use the cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2, PDB 4EK3) and a ligand from PDB 1YKR. The files 4EK3_rec.pdbqt and 1YKR_lig.pdbqt are available in the tutorial data file.
Start the graphical interface with ADFRsuite-1.0/bin/agfrgui.

3. Define box
Click  to make the docking box cover the ligand, click on  to focus the 3D scene on the box, and click  to label residues in the box.
The docking box is now centered on the ligand and scaled to have a 4.0 angstroms padding from the ligand atoms.
The padding can be adjusted using the spin box in the “docking box” section.

This particular ligand overlaps with side chains of the receptor’s apo conformation. Label the receptor residues in the docking box by clicking in the  button in the tool bar, and zoom in and rotate to observe the overlap of lysine 33 and lysine 89 with the ligand.

title: Tutorial: maps for flexible receptor side chains
text:
4. Make side chains flexible
Click on  and select LYS33 and LYS89
A residue selection widget displays all receptor amino acids currently in the docking box and having a side chain that can adopt multiple conformations (i.e. not alanine, glycine or proline). Check the box for a residue to select it for having its side chain made flexible during the docking. Side chains selected as flexible for docking are displayed in the 3D view as orange Sticks & Balls and listed in the type in widget.

Notes:

If a ligand has been loaded, receptor side chains to be made flexible can also be selected based on their distance from the ligand by checking the “residue within” button. Checking this button will override the current selection with the set of receptor side chains having at least one moving side chain atom within the current distance cutoff (i.e. 3.0 Angstroms in this case) of the ligand. Keep in mind that the more side chains are made flexible the harder the docking problem. While ADFR has no hard limit on how many side-chains can be made flexible we recommend keeping the number below 10 to 15.
The receptor amino acids selected to have flexible side-chains during the docking calculation are now listed in the type-in widget.  along with the number such residues. Flexible residues can be specified manually by typing directly in this widget. A residue can be specified by its residue number (e.g. “89”), or by its residue type and number (e.g.“LYS89”). Multiple residues must be separated by a comma ‘,’ or space characters, optionally preceded by a chain id (i.e. “A:120,LYS89”). If the chain id is omitted matching residues from all chains are selected. Residues from different chains can be specified by separating the selection string for each chain by a semi colon ‘;’ e.g. “A:10,24,35;B:12,34”
Close the interface by destroying the window, using the button in the corner of the window.

title: Tutorial: maps for flexible receptor side chains
text:
7. Binding pockets
Click on 
Ligand binding pockets are computed using AutoSite by identifying and clustering high-affinity points. Each cluster of points is called a “fill” and listed in the table widget. The pocket with the largest AutoSite score is selected by default and displayed as a set of green dots. The fill points of all selected fills are displayed in the 3D viewer and will be written into the target files.
Notes:

the “Pocket” status light is now green
the “generate target file …” is enabled.

title: Tutorial: maps for flexible receptor side chains
text:
8. Maps parameters
Check the  button
loading the ligand initialized the list of maps to be computed to the list of AutoDock atom types found in the ligand, in this case: “A C Cl HD N NA OA”. Computing maps for all atoms types will use a little more disk space but the resulting target file can be used for any ligand and is recommended.

The “edit …” button will display an interface for manually specifying the list of atoms types for which affinity maps are requested.
Water maps: water maps are calculated automatically and stored in the target file. These maps are used for hydrated docking. Their parameters can be set in the “water map setting” pull-down.

Gradients: By default, an affinity gradient will be created for the region of the grid covered by the receptor (except for the electrostatic and desolvation maps). If your CPU has multiple cores and OpenMP is detected, the calculation will execute in parallel and the number of available threads appears in the GUI title bar. Gradients are not required, however, they are recommended as they have been shown to help docking find solutions more efficiently. The addition of gradients requires the definition of the interior and exterior of the receptor. By default, the largest cluster of negative values (favorable affinities) is used to define the exterior of the receptor. In this case, everything else, including receptor cavities large enough to hold solvent but not open to the solvent, will be considered the interior and will be overwritten with the gradient. To prevent the gradient generation on grid points of internal cavities, the user can specify a cluster size above which clusters of points with negative values are considered to be outside the receptor and therefore preserve their original affinity values.

title: Tutorial: maps for flexible receptor side chains
text:
9. Generate maps
Click on the “generate target file…” button, name the target file as 4EK3_FR33_88_89
The program asks for the name and location for the target file that will be generated. It will then compute the affinity maps and store them in the target file along with meta data.

The generated target file describes the binding pocket targeted for docking on the receptor. It stores the PDBQT file of the receptor used to compute the affinity maps, the grid parameter file used to run AutoGrid, as well as files generated by the AutoGrid run (i.e. affinity maps, AutoGrid log file, etc.). In addition, it stores meta-data about the generation of the target file such as: the time and computer architecture on which the maps were computed, the docking-box parameters, the grid parameter file, the versions of AGFR and AutoSite, the water map parameters, etc.
It is recommended to use names that are descriptive. In this case we use 4EK3_FR33_88_89.
Pressing the “Save” button will start the calculation in a separate thread, leaving the graphical user interface responsive. The progress bar below the button will indicate the level of completion of the calculation.

Note: a target file can be inspected from the command line using the about command (ADFRsuite-1.0/bin/about)

The “Cov” status button in the status bar becomes enabled .

title: Tutorial: maps for covalent docking
text:
5. First atom
Pick CB in CYS164 as the first atom of the covalent bond (left mouse button click) .
As an atom is picked in the 3D viewer, a small sphere is displayed on the picked atom, the atom name is displayed in the atom 1 field, and the mouse function is set to picking the second atom.

Notes:

clicking on the arrow button to the right of the “atom 1” and “atom 2” fields set the left mouse picking function of the 3D viewer to pick the corresponding atom.
The visibility of the spheres highlighting the covalent bond is toggled using the  button in the toolbar.

title: Tutorial: maps for covalent docking
text:
6. Second atom
pick SG in CYS164 as the second atom of the covalent bond
As the second atom forming the covalent bond is picked, a small sphere is displayed on the picked atom, the picked atom name is displayed in the “atom 2” field, and the sub-graph rooted at the covalent bond (atom1 atom2) is displayed with dashed lines, outlining the atoms identified as the covalent ligand (if any). These atoms will be removed from the receptor when calculating the affinity maps. The list of removed atoms appears in the dialog.
The left mouse picking function in the 3D viewer is now assigned to editing the set of atoms in the covalent ligand. Clicking on an included atom (i.e. with dashed lines) will exclude it and vice versa.

Notes:

In some cases the covalent ligand has a second covalent bond with the receptor (due to close contacts) which leads to a covalent ligand that includes potentially large parts of the receptor. The “limit cov. Lig.” field in the dialog allows to address this issue by limiting the traversal of the receptor molecule to a list of residues. For instance, typing A:CYS164,HMY1 in this field will limit the traversal to the ligand and these 2 residues prevent the erroneous inclusion of other receptor amino acids in the set of atoms considered to be the covalent ligand.
The “Start over” button will clear the dialog and let you start over.
If the second atom picked is not covalently bound to the first picked atom, a dialog is displayed asking whether or not to proceed. The dialog show the atoms identity as well as the distance between these atoms helping the user decide whether they picked the right atom or not and whether to proceed or not. This feature is useful when the covalent bond happens to be too long for a bond to be created in the viewer.
Click OK on the dialog once the proper covalent bond was defined and the set of atoms to be removed (i.e. the covalent ligand) is correct.
The “Cov” status light is now green and the pocket validity light is disabled as no fill points are needed for covalent docking.

title: Tutorial: maps for covalent docking
text:
7. Maps parameters
Check the  button
By default maps for all known AutoDock atom types will be computed. This is recommended as it will use a little more disk space but the resulting target file can be used for any ligand.

The “edit …” button will display an interface for manually specifying the list of atoms types for which affinity maps are requested. The C OA and HD maps are always calculated as they are used to compute the water map.
Water maps: water maps are calculated automatically and stored in the target file. These maps are used for hydrated docking. Their parameters can be set in the “water map setting” pull-down.

Gradients: By default, an affinity gradient will be created for the region of the grid covered by the receptor (except for the electrostatic and desolvation maps). If your CPU has multiple cores and OpenMP is detected, the calculation will execute in parallel and the number of available threads appears in the GUI title bar. Gradients are not required, however, they are recommended as they have been shown to help docking find solutions more efficiently. The addition of gradients requires the definition of the interior and exterior of the receptor. By default, the largest cluster of negative values (favorable affinities) is used to define the exterior of the receptor. In this case, everything else, including receptor cavities large enough to hold solvent but not open to the solvent, will be considered the interior and will be overwritten with the gradient. To prevent the gradient generation on grid points of internal cavities, the user can specify a cluster size above which clusters of points with negative values are considered to be outside the receptor and therefore preserve their original affinity values.

title: Tutorial: maps for covalent docking
text:
8. Generate maps
Click on the “generate target file…” button
The program asks for the name and location for the target file that will be generated. It will then compute the affinity maps and store them in the target file along with meta data.

The generated target file describes the binding pocket targeted for docking on the receptor. It stores the PDBQT file of the receptor used to compute the affinity maps, the grid parameter file used to run AutoGrid, as well as files generated by the AutoGrid run (i.e. affinity maps, AutoGrid log file, etc.). In addition, it stores meta-data about the generation of the target file such as: the time and computer architecture on which the maps were computed, the docking-box parameters, the grid parameter file, the versions of AGFR and AutoSite, the water map parameters, etc.
Pressing the “Save” button will start the calculation in a separate thread, leaving the graphical user interface responsive. The progress bar below the button will indicate the level of completion of the calculation.

title: AutoGridFR (AGFR)
text:
AutoGridFR (AGFR) computes the affinity maps that AutoDockFR, AutoDock CrankPep and AutoDock4 use to represent the binding site of a receptor during docking. AGFR is part of ADFRsuite.
AGFR can set the position and size of the docking box in several ways, from the command line or from a graphical user interface. It runs AutoGrid4 to calculate the affinity maps and stores them in a target file (.trg) together with metadata that describe the maps and how they were calculated. The metadata make maps easier to manage and support data provenance and reproducibility. Target files can be unzipped and the maps extracted for use with AutoDock4.

title: AutoSite
text:
AutoSite identifies and characterizes binding sites in macromolecules of known three-dimensional structure (the receptor). It finds binding sites by clustering high-affinity points; each cluster corresponds to a potential binding pocket.
Points within a cluster are labeled by their preference for hydrophobic ligand atoms or for hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor ligand atoms, which gives a “colored” description of the pocket. From these colored points AutoSite derives a set of putative positions for hydrophobic and hydrogen-bonding ligand atoms, called feature points.
In the published benchmark, AutoSite outperformed state-of-the-art energy- and geometry-based methods at identifying the binding sites of known ligands. For the 85 ligands of the Astex Diverse Set, it placed feature points of the right type within 2.0 Å of 79% of hydrophobic ligand atoms, of 81% of hydrogen-bond acceptor ligand atoms bonded to the receptor, and of 63% of hydrogen atoms forming hydrogen bonds with the receptor.

ADFR docks the ligand into the receptor while treating the 2 side chains A:ILE10 and A:LYS33 as flexible. adfr detects the available cores and uses all of them by default. Here it runs 8 independent searches (--nbRuns 8), each with up to 20,000 evaluations of the scoring function (--maxEvals 20000). By default adfr runs 50 searches of 2.5 million evaluations each. Harder docking problems need more searches to raise the chance of finding the best pose (the global minimum of the scoring function). The low values here give a quick run that is enough to show how docking works.

Output files are named after the ligand, followed by the job name (--jobName, if given).
The search is stochastic: docking the same ligand into the same target twice can give different results with different random seeds. Setting the seed (--seed) makes a run reproducible for a given version of the code. See the re-docking tutorial for details.

For covalent docking, the receptor and the covalent ligand must share 3 atoms, as shown below: 2 atoms (green) form the covalent bond, and 1 atom (yellow) is an anchor on the receptor side. These atoms are used to move the ligand into place relative to the receptor and create the covalent bond.

Details:

The box position and size are set by hand here to show this option. This is the only -b/--boxMode option that ignores padding.
-c/--covalentBond gives the serial numbers of the 2 receptor atoms that form the covalent bond, as they appear in the PDBQT file.
-t/--covalentBondTorsionAtom gives the third atom of the covalent attachment, used to compute the torsion angle of the covalent bond.
-x/--covalentResidues limits the traversal of the receptor to a list of residues. This is sometimes needed because covalent ligands can form bonds with the receptor other than the covalent attachment, as the native ligand of 3C9W does. When agfr walks the sub-tree beyond the covalent bond to find which atoms to cut out of the receptor for the affinity maps, that spurious bond would make it include a large part of the receptor, cutting out more than 1600 atoms. -x prevents this.

title: AutoDockFR (ADFR)
text:
AutoDockFR (ADFR) is a protein–ligand docking program developed in the Sanner laboratory at Scripps Research under the AutoDock umbrella. It uses:
ADFR supports the docking modes of AutoDock4 and Vina, but it was designed specifically to include selective receptor flexibility, and it also supports covalent docking. Its custom genetic algorithm can dock ligands with more rotatable bonds than AutoDock4. ADFR is distributed as part of the ADFR software suite, which provides additional tools for automated docking.

title: AutoDockFR (ADFR)
text:
Ease of use
ADFR streamlines the docking procedure and supports managing and reproducing docking experiments through data provenance. Self-documenting files store:

the binding-pocket representation used for docking (target files, .trg), and
the docking results (Docking Result Object files, .dro).

The metadata in these files supports reproducibility and reduces the risk of operator errors, such as mixing up affinity maps.

title: AutoDockFR (ADFR)
text:
Input

Ligands are prepared for docking with AutoDock, in the PDBQT format; ADFR derives the ligand’s flexibility from its rotatable bonds. prepare_ligand converts a ligand PDB file to PDBQT.
The receptor is given as a target file, a single file describing the receptor. Target files are computed from a receptor PDBQT file with agfr on the command line or with the graphical interface agfrgui (see AutoGridFR). prepare_receptor converts a receptor PDB file to PDBQT; see how to create a PDBQT file for a receptor.

title: AutoDockFR (ADFR)
text:
Usage
Given a receptor and a ligand in PDBQT format, a simple docking runs like this:
agfr -r rec.pdbqt -l xtallig.pdbqt -o target
adfr -t target.trg -l lig.pdbqt -J firstDocking
Line 1 uses the native ligand xtallig.pdbqt of receptor rec.pdbqt to define a docking box covering the pocket and computes the AutoDock affinity maps, stored in target.trg. Line 2 docks the ligand lig.pdbqt into this pocket. More examples are in the tutorials.

title: AutoDockFR (ADFR)
text:
Implementation
ADFR is written in object-oriented languages and built from reusable software components. Performance-critical components are in C and C++ (for example ADFRcc); others are in Python (ADFR, AutoSite, MolKit2, ProDy). See Implementation for the list of components.

This tutorial re-docks a known ligand into its native receptor: one of the ligands of cyclin-dependent kinase 2, CDK2 (PDB 4EK4), into the CDK2 structure PDB 4EK3.
You will learn to:
Prerequisites: ADFRsuite 1.0 installed with ADFRsuite-1.0/bin on your PATH, and the tutorial data downloaded and unzipped (see Tutorials). Run the commands from the folder that contains data/.

1. Generate the target file
agfr -r data/4EK3_rec.pdbqt -l data/4EK4_lig.pdbqt -o ligPocket
You can also use agfrgui and follow the AGFR box around a ligand tutorial.



Option
Meaning




-r
the receptor file (required)


-l
the ligand file


-o
name for the target file



Details. agfr positions and sizes the docking box over the receptor pocket(s) where the ligand will be docked, and computes affinity maps for a list of AutoDock4 atom types. The maps are calculated by AutoGrid4.

Box. The box can be set in several ways with -b/--boxMode. Here agfr uses the bounding box of the known ligand (-l/--ligand), with 4 Å of padding added on every side. Change the padding with -P/--padding.
Output. The target file (.trg) is saved under the name given by -o/--output; without it, a unique descriptive name is created. It contains the affinity maps, translational points for placing the ligand at sensible positions in the box, and metadata about the grid size, position and spacing, the receptor atoms involved and the maps. Inspect it with the about command.
Pockets. The translational points are computed by AutoSite, which clusters high-affinity grid points into potential binding pockets. -p/--pocketMode sets how multiple clusters are handled; when it is omitted, as here, all clusters are merged into one set of translational points.
Atom types. By default maps are computed for all AutoDock4 atom types. Restrict them with -m/--mapTypes for smaller files and faster runs, but the target file then cannot dock ligands with atom types it has no map for.

Exercise: re-dock the ligand reliably
The command
adfr -l data/4EK4_random.pdbqt -t ligPocket.trg --jobName rigid --nbRuns 8 --maxEvals 20000 -O --seed 1

With the command above, every search ended while it was still improving its solutions. The natural first step is therefore to give each search more evaluations so it can converge. 1. Convert PDB files to PDBQT files
PDBQT is the file format of the AutoDock programs. It adds two columns to the PDB format: the partial charge and the AutoDock atom type.
We start from two separate PDB files for the receptor and the peptide, split from the 3Q47 entry. Both contain only protein atoms.
Unzip the data and go to the directory for this tutorial:

cd ADCP_tutorial_data/3Q47

title: Tutorial: re-docking a 7-mer peptide
text:
2. Generate the target file
A target file is a zipped file with everything needed for docking with ADFR and ADCP. It can be generated from the command line or a GUI.
agfr -r 3Q47_recH.pdbqt -l 3Q47_pepH.pdbqt -asv 1.1 -o 3Q47
This puts the docking box around the given peptide with 4 Å padding. If you do not know the peptide binding site, see the agfrgui tutorials.







Option
Meaning




-r
the receptor file (required)


-l
the ligand file


-asv
AutoSite version, 1.0 or 1.1 (default 1.0 when -asv is not given)


-o
name for the target file



Details. agfr positions and sizes the docking box over the receptor pocket(s) where the ligand will be docked, and computes affinity maps for a list of AutoDock4 atom types. The maps are calculated by AutoGrid4.

Box. The box can be set in several ways with -b/--boxMode. Here agfr uses the bounding box of the known ligand (-l/--ligand), with 4 Å of padding added on every side. Change the padding with -P/--padding.
Output. The target file (.trg) is saved under the name given by -o/--output; without it, a unique descriptive name is created. It contains the affinity maps, translational points for placing the ligand at sensible positions in the box, and metadata about the grid size, position and spacing, the receptor atoms involved and the maps. Inspect it with the about command.
Pockets. The translational points are computed by AutoSite, which clusters high-affinity grid points into potential binding pockets. -p/--pocketMode sets how multiple clusters are handled; when it is omitted, as here, all clusters are merged into one set of translational points.
Atom types. By default maps are computed for all AutoDock4 atom types. Restrict them with -m/--mapTypes for smaller files and faster runs, but the target file then cannot dock ligands with atom types it has no map for.

text:
3. Dock the peptide from its sequence
adcp -t 3Q47.trg -s npisdvd -N 20 -n 1000000 -o 3Q47_redocking -ref 3Q47_pepH.pdb
adcp detects the available cores and uses all of them by default. Here it runs 20 independent searches (-N, --nbRuns 20), each with up to 1,000,000 evaluations of the scoring function (-n, --numSteps). By default adcp runs 50 searches of 2.5 million evaluations each. Harder docking problems need more searches to raise the chance of finding the best pose (the global minimum of the scoring function).
The run writes:







File
Content




3Q47_redocking_ranked_*.pdb
final solutions, ranked after clustering


3Q47_redocking_*.pdb
the Monte Carlo trajectory of each replica


3Q47_redocking_*.out
detailed output of each replica









TipNotes




The search is stochastic: docking the same peptide into the same target twice can give different results with different random seeds. The energy landscape is the same in both runs; if both find its global minimum they give the same solution, whatever path the search took. Searches trapped in local minima give different poses. Setting the seed (--seed) makes a run reproducible for a given version of the code.
In general, run 100 replicas with 1 million steps per amino acid, starting from a mixture of extended and helical conformations.

text:
Run ADCP with modified amino acids
adcp -T 3Q47.trg -s "n<BHD>pis&dvd" -N 2 -n 2000 -L swiss -w testDir -o testNSAAandD
In version 1.1 the peptide sequence can contain non-natural amino acids, written as [&]x<NAME>:

The optional & makes the amino acid D instead of the default L chirality.
x is the coarse bead that represents the side chain. Any one-letter code of a natural amino acid can be used here.
The modified side chain’s name goes between chevrons, <>.

In the example, the first amino acid is represented as an asparagine in the coarse model, and an asparagine derivative side chain (BHD) from the Swiss side-chain library is used for the full-atom representation. The peptide also contains a D-aspartic acid at position 5.






Tip



The modified side chain is loaded from a library file, here the Swiss library selected with -L swiss.


This example runs only 2 Monte Carlo searches (-N 2) of 2000 evaluations each, so that it finishes quickly; it is not meant to find real docked poses. It writes two files into the working directory testDir (-w):

-env implicit

-dr

-reint

Minimizing poses that are already docked

Post-docking minimization (-pdmin) applies OpenMM minimization to poses that were already docked. ADCP skips docking and minimizes the poses from the earlier output file. Use the same target file (-T), job name (-o) and sequence (-s) as in the docking run.
Resume a failed minimization (-resumemin) continues an interrupted minimization and re-ranking. It works only together with -pdmin and without overwriting (-O).



Non-standard amino acids
The default force-field parameters for OpenMM minimization lack most non-standard amino acids. ADCP therefore uses the “sannerlab” OpenMM parameter set for 182 non-standard amino acids and the “swiss” set for 20 non-terminal ones. These sets are designed for the Swiss non-standard amino acids and need proper licensing from the developer of the SwissSideChain database. The full list of supported residues is in ADCP/data/openMMff/AVAILABLE_PARAMETER.dat.
When no OpenMM parameters exist for a non-standard amino acid, ADCP uses pdbfixer (v1.8) to replace it with a standard one. If pdbfixer cannot replace it, the residue is mutated to alanine for the OpenMM re-ranking.







Option
Meaning




-F
which OpenMM parameter sets to use from ADCP/data/openMMff (swiss, sannerlab or none); none turns off all system default sets


-f
user-supplied OpenMM parameters for new or unlisted non-standard amino acids (see below)



-f needs three files in the same directory with the same stem. For -f ./XXXX_ff.xml the program expects a force-field file ./XXXX_ff.xml, a bond definition file ./XXXX_residues.xml and a hydrogen definition file ./XXXX_hydrogen_def.xml.

title: ADCP 1.1 documentation
text:
Non-canonical amino acids
ADCP 1.1 docks peptides that contain non-natural amino acids (NSAAs). Each NSAA has a name (for example PTR), and ADCP reads its side-chain parameters from library files given on the command line (-l and -L). ADCP ships with a library for the natural amino acids (always loaded) and a library of fluorinated amino acids.
We also developed parameters for all amino acids of SwissSideChain. Its license will be replaced by CC-BY 4.0, and we have been granted the right to distribute the ADCP library for this set of 209 amino acids in D and L forms.
The library covers 182 of the 209 SwissSideChain amino acids, in both L and D chirality. This lets ADCP handle every non-natural amino acid currently found in the Protein Data Bank. To use peptides with NSAAs at any position in OpenMM, we:

Computed partial charges. SwissSideChain’s charges were designed for NSAAs away from the peptide termini, so we computed charges for terminal and non-terminal forms with the R.E.D. server (RESP ESP charge Derive), using GAMESS, following this tutorial. Each form was capped with ACE and/or NME.
Found force-field parameters. parmchk2 from AmberTools identified the Amber parameters needed (bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers, electrostatics, van der Waals) from the R.E.D. mol2 files, written as an frcmod file.
Built FFXML files. ParmEd converted the frcmod and mol2 files into OpenMM FFXML files for each variant. These were merged into one file covering all parameters for 184 NSAAs, which OpenMM can load.

To use these parameters in OpenMM we also changed how each structure is loaded, cleaned and simulated:

Kept pdbfixer from removing or swapping NSAAs, by loading the residue definition file and editing pdbfixer.nonstandardResidues.
Added OXT to C-terminal NSAAs. pdbfixer adds hydrogens with Modeller and handles N-terminal residues correctly, but not terminal NSAAs.
Overrode the default hydrogen definitions, to add NSAA-specific ones or apply specific parameter sets to residues with identical names (for example ORN).
Gave residues with identical molecular structures (for example THR and ALO) their own residue templates.
Overrode PDB writing to handle 4-letter residue codes, with a modified PDB writer.

title: Beaded ribbons
text:
With Pmv 1.5.6 we introduced a new Ribbon model called “beaded Ribbon”. This model provides a smooth transition between coils, strands and helices.
The model is made of cylinders for coils and turns that seamlessly merge into sheets for helices and strands. All aspects of this representation can be controlled by the user. The command is invoked through the Compute menu:

The beaded ribbon will be computed for all molecules in the current selection (or all molecules in Pmv if nothing is selected) using the default set of parameters

A Graphical User Interface (GUI) is provided allowing modifying the various parameters defining the representation.
The “general” panel of the GUI defines the overall quality, which specifies the number of points per residue used for representing the ribbon. The taperLength parameter indicates how many such points are used to morph between cylinders in coils and turns, and the start of strands and start and end of helices. Finally, for molecules providing secondary structure information in the file they were read from, this panel offers a choice of secondary structure element definition based on the information in the file or assigned programmatically using PROSS.

The Coils panel provides access to coils and turns related parameters. Since coils and turns are represented using a single cylinder, the only parameters are the cylinder radius and the color.

The Helix panel provides control over Helix related parameters, including the width of the 2 sheets and their colors (inside sheet and outside sheet). The beads (i.e. the 2 cylinders flanking the sheets) can be turned off by un-checking the “Beads” check button. This will hide the controls for the Beads parameters. When beads are displayed, the radius can be set using the thumbwheel and the color of each bead can be set using the color picker buttons.
Likewise, the thickness (i.e. the distance between the 2 sheets) can be controlled through a thumbwheel. When the Thickness check button is un-checked, this control is hidden and there will be a single polygonal sheet displayed.

The Sheet panel provides control over parameters defining the rendering of strands in beta sheets. The body of the arrow representing a strand is located between the end of the initial taper and the base of the arrowhead. The width at the beginning and the end of the body can be set along with the colors used for either side of the sheet, using the top row of controls. The additional three groups of control allow to specify whether or not beads, arrowhead, and double faces are drawn or not. When these elements are drawn (i.e. the check button is checked) controls allow specifying bead radius and color of the bead on either side, separation between the 2 sides of the sheet (i.e. thickness), and the length of the arrowhead (in number of points) and the width at the base of the arrow head.

The last panel in the GUI provides a series of check buttons, one for each sheet. Checking and un-checking these buttons allows swapping the first and second side allowing to achieve uniform coloring of outside and inside faces in a TIM barrel structure for instance.
NOTE: the current implementation does not allow this geometry to be printed as a 3D model.
NOTE: Unlike the traditional ribbon representation, which can be displayed for any subset of residues, the beaded ribbon geometry cannot be displayed for less than a molecule.

title: Dashboard
text:
With Pmv 1.5.6 we introduce a completely re-designed dashboard widget that facilitates carrying out Pmv commands that previously required navigating through several menus and forms with a single click. This interface presents molecules and molecular fragments in a tree structure. The matrix of buttons to the right of the tree is used to carry out the Pmv command corresponding to the column on the molecular fragment corresponding to the line. For instance, in the picture below, the crosshair is on the ‘S’ column which is the Pmv selection command and the chain ‘B’ line under protease, a protein loaded in Pmv. As the tooltip indicates, clicking a first time on this square button will select the chain B of protease. Clicking a second time on this button will deselect the entire protein.

The Pmv commands mapped to the columns of buttons are: select  , display lines  , display balls and sticks  , display CPK  , display Ribbon  , display molecular surface  , display labels  , and color  commands. Tooltips indicate the function of each button.
There are three types of buttons in the Dashboard. The first type  is a stateless button with 2 functions: the green circle carries out the command (i.e. select, display, label) while the red circle negates the command (i.e. deselect, undisplay, unlabel).
The second type of buttons (e.g.  ,  ,   ,  ) show the fraction of the group for which the state is on. In the picture above, all of protease is displayed as lines so there are full solid red circles in the display line column, while only chain A is displayed as balls and sticks so the circle for chain A displayed as balls and sticks is solid while the circle for balls and sticks for protease is ½ solid (i.e. 1 chain out of 2). Clicking on a button that has less than 100% of its children on forces the command on all children. Clicking on a button that is completely on (solid) negates the command. In other words, the cycle is  ⇒  ⇒  ⇒  … where ⇒ represents clicking on the button.
In general, left clicking on a button carries out the command with default parameters, while right click opens an option panel specific to the command. However, there are exceptions. For instance, the menu buttons for labeling and coloring have no action associated with the right click event while the selection command has a selection menu associated with the right click.

Molecular Fragment menu
Right clicking in a molecular fragment in the tree widget will bring up a menu that will vary based on the fragment. For instance, right clicking on “Pmv Molecules” triggers the read molecule command that displays a file browser for selecting a molecular file to read. Right clicking in “Current Selection” offers the options: to split the selection (i.e. make the current selection a different molecule) or to show the selection in the 3D Viewer by translating and scaling the scene. Right clicking on a molecule displays a longer menu with options to delete the molecule, view the text file from which the molecule was read, etc…


Working with the ‘Current Selection’
Pmv has powerful commands for creating selections. In the dashboard, one can type selection strings  to create a selection or use the button in the left most column  . The line of buttons located to the right of ‘Current Selection in the tree  supports operations on the current selection. Note that there is no button on in the Select column of that line, since selecting the current selection does not do anything.


Creating custom sets

A Pmv selection can be saved as a new line in the Dashboard to facilitate rapid Dashboard-based operations on this specific subset. This is done using the  button in the upper left corner. When this button is clicked on and there is a selection, a dialog is displayed asking for a name for the set.Clicking ‘OK’ in this dialog will add a line to the dashboard tree widget  .
Sets can be renamed or removed through the menu obtained by right clicking on the set name in the tree widget.


Configuring the Dashboard
The button located above the tree widget sets the dashboard width so that all command columns are visible (  ), increases the size of the command button (  ), and decreases the size of the command buttons (  ). Note that the height of the lines in the tree is fixed, which causes the circles to become ovals for large button sizes.


The selection command menu

This menu is obtained by right clicking on the buttons in the select command column. It allows the user to tailor the selection by specifying groups of atoms to add or remove from the selection. By default, atoms are added to the selection. To remove parts of the selection, first check the ‘Deselect’ button then specify the atom set using the next five entries, which are shortcuts for selecting common subsets of atoms. Here, Hetero Atoms are the atoms from HETATM records in PDB files.
The following 6 sets are predefined as follows:

water: residue name is WAT or HOH
Ions: residue name is in the list http://decogroup.org/ion_list.txt
DNA: residue name is one of DC, DG, DA, DT, DI, or N.
RNA: residue name is one of C, G, A, U, I, N.
Amino Acids: residue name is one of ALA, CYS, ASP, GLU, PHE, GLY, HIS, ILE, LYS, LEU, MET, ASN, PRO, GLN, ARG, SER, THR, VAL, TRP, TYR, or the residue name is declared as a modified residue in the PDB file using a MODRES record. Common example of such names are: HID, HSP, HIE, HIP, CYX, CSS, ACE, MSE, 5HP, SOC.
Ligand: anything that is not water, Ions, DNA, RNA or an amino acid.

In addition this menu supports selecting atoms based on their current representation. In this particular case, the atoms are displayed as lines, spheres as well as balls and sticks. The list of options in this section will change based on the representation that are displayed.
The last section for expanding the selection and selecting around the current selection will only appear if there is a current selection. Expanding the selection will select atoms located within a user-specified distance from any currently selected atom. As the cutoff is modified, cyan colored spheres show what would be selected for the current cutoff value. The selection expands only to atoms belonging to the molecular fragment on the line on which the selection menu was activated. In the picture below, the current selection is the small molecule (indinavir). The menu was activated on protease in order to expand the selection atoms in protease. Once the “Expand selection” menu entry is activated, a counter is displayed with a cutoff value that can be modified. The selection operation is performed by clicking on the green button to the right of the cutoff value or cancelled using the red button.
Select around behaves the same as expand selection but will deselect the current selection and only keep the atoms in the vicinity of the current selection selected.



Coloring Menu

The coloring menu will list all current representations for the molecular fragment on which the menu is invoked. In this case, protease has cpk spheres, balls and sticks, lines and a protein label. Note that the coloring menu entries are disabled as currently no representation has been selected. If there were only one representation available, its check button would be checked by default when the menu was displayed.
Once at least one representation to be colored has been selected, the coloring commands in the menu become active.
The first two coloring commands are (1) color by atom type using a user modifiable atom type color palette, and (2) color by polarity according to a scheme developed by David Goodsell, in which carbon atoms are colored white, polar oxygens are colored pink and charged oxygens are colored red, polar nitrogen are colored light blue and charged nitrogen are colored bright blue, sulfur and phosphorus are yellow, and hydrogens are colored the same as the atoms they are bonded to.
The next set of 8 coloring commands have an additional option, which is to choose to apply the coloring scheme only to the carbon atoms in the molecular fragment on which the menu was invoked. Choose color opens a color picker widget to use to pick a color. Color by molecule and by chain will color each molecule or chain differently using a user-modifiable palette. Color by residue type uses predefined amino acid colors. Color by rainbow performs an N to C coloring along the molecule’s sequence using a rainbow colormap. Color Chains by Rainbow will only appear if the menu is invoked on a molecule. It will apply the rainbow map to each chain in the protein.


Labeling

The Labeling menu lets the user add and remove atom, residue, chain or molecule labels. Full labels are composed of 4 strings separated by colons MolName : ChainName : ResidueName : AtomName.

title: Geometry tools
text:
The Geometry Tools group provides a way for the user to set common rendering attributes for geometries displayed in the 3D Viewer. A tree widget reveals a “root” object, which is the parent of every geometry displayed in Pmv. This widget is used to select a geometrical object for which rendering attributes will be modified using the Appearance Tools and Clipping planes interfaces located below the tree. Note that when no geometry is selected, the appearance and clipping planes widgets are disabled.
Every molecule loaded in Pmv creates a child of the root object named after the molecule (e.g. 1crn). The children of the molecule node are the geometrical objects displayed in the 3D Viewer to represent this molecule in various ways. This list may vary based on the representations calculated and shown for a particular molecule. Nodes in this tree can be expanded and collapsed by clicking on the blue triangular shape located to the left of the node’s name.
A geometrical object is selected by clicking on its name. A yellow background identifies the current geometrical object.
Once a geometrical object is selected the “Appearance panel” lets the user specify whether this object should be rendered with front and/or back faces as well as which rendering mode (points, lines, Gouraud shaded, Outlines Gouraud shaded) is used for front and for back facing polygons as well as the color and opacity of the front and back polygons of this geometrical object.
The top row of buttons in the Appearance Tools group pertains to the front facing polygons (i.e. polygons with a normal vector pointing toward the camera or person viewing the scene). The first button  toggles the visibility of front facing polygons and is on by default. The next 4 buttons respectively set the rendering of front facing polygons to: points  , lines  , Gouraud shaded  and outlined Gouraud shaded  . For point and line rendering, right clicking on the button opens an interface for setting rendering parameters such as point and line width  . Numerical values can be typed in or incremented and decremented using the counter widget’s arrows. Clicking on the green check button sets the value and dismisses the interface, while clicking on the red button dismisses the interface without setting the value. The last button in the row  invokes the color chooser. The opacity thumbwheel is used to set the opacity of the front facing polygons. The second row of buttons performs the same functions for the back facing polygons.
The “Clipping Planes” group provides an interface for enabling/disabling, transforming and capping arbitrary clipping planes. The 3D Viewer in Pmv supports up to 6 arbitrary clipping planes, each of which can be enabled or disabled for any geometrical object displayed in PMV. By default when a clipping plane is enabled it will clip all children geometries. Clipping planes 1 through 6 are enabled using the middle row button. The top row of buttons supports binding the 3D viewer’s virtual trackball used to create 3D transformations such as translations and rotations to a given clipping plane. When a clipping plane is transformed, its graphical representation is drawn in the 3D Viewer. Moreover, a red button is added at the right end of the top row, which can be used to stop transforming the clipping plane and restore transformation of the 3D scene. The left mouse button rotates the clipping plane. The right mouse button translates the clipping plane in X and Y screen coordinates. Shift right translates the plane along its normal.

The last row of buttons is used to “cap” a particular clipping plane. Currently capping only works properly if the edge of the clipped geometrical object has a single connected component. It is possible to use multiple clipping planes on the same geometry with caps. The caps appear in the 3D Viewer as children of the clipped geometrical object, thus allowing control over the rendering of the caps.

title: Selection strings
text:
Among the various ways molecular fragments can be selected in Pmv, selection strings are one of the most powerful selection mechanisms.
Pmv stores molecules in a hierarchical data structure with 4 levels: Molecules contains Chains, made of Residues, containing Atoms. A Pmv selection string is a :-separated set of 1 to 4 expressions where the first expression will select one or more molecules, the second expression if present will select chains among these molecules, the 3rd expression will select residues in these chains, and finally the 4th expression if present will select atoms in the previously selected residues. The result of such a selection will be a set of Molecules, Chains, Residues, or Atoms depending on the number of expressions.
Mol selector [: [Chain selector] [: [Residue selector] [: [Atom selector]]]]
Multiple selection strings can be combined, separated by ;.

Expressions syntax
Expressions can be strings, sometimes numbers or ranges of numbers, or lambda expressions (i.e. a Python function with no name).
An empty string selects everything. For example:
::: will select all Atoms in all Residues in all Chains in all Molecules in Pmv
Mol1:: will select all Residues in all Chains in molecule Mol1
Mol2:B:: will select all atoms in Chain B in molecule Mol2
A comma-separated list of items can be used in an expression. For instance:
Mol1, Mol2:::C,N,CA,O selects backbone heavy atoms in molecules Mol1 and Mol2
A Range can be specified using the - character.
::ALA35-THR45 selects a range of residues
1CRN-2PLV selects all molecules in the list of molecules loaded in Pmv starting at and including 1CRN and ending and including 2PLV. This will only work if 1CRN was loaded before 2PLV. Else an empty set is returned.
Expressions can contain common regular expressions such as . to match any single character, * to match any number of any character, and [1235] to match the numbers 1 through five in a single position.
::..N* selects all Residues with the third letter in its name being an N followed by any string
::...[23]. selects all Residues with names made of exactly 5 characters and where the 4th character is either 2 or 3
Relative positions in a list can be indicated by using the # symbol in front of a number.
#2,#5 selects the 2nd and 5th molecule
Mol1:C:#1-#5 selects the first 5 Residues in Chain C of molecule Mol1
Names of predefined sets can also be used in expressions. Names will be matched at the level of the elements they contain. A list of standard predefined set names is available here. Sets defined by the user will be matched as well.


Molecule selectors
Molecular selectors match the expression against the molecule names. They support regular expressions, relative indices, lists and ranges.


Chain selectors
Chain selectors match the expression against the chain’s id. They support regular expressions, relative indices, lists and ranges.


Residue selectors
Residue selectors usually match the expression against the Residue name, which is a concatenation of the 3-letter Residue type (e.g. ALA, TYR, etc) and the Residue number from the PDB file (e.g. 3, 4A, etc.). One letter amino acid code can also be used (available here). Regular expressions, relative indices, lists, and ranges are supported.


Atom selectors
Atom selectors match the expression against the atom name. Regular expressions, relative indices, lists, and ranges are supported.


Where to use selection strings
Selection strings can be used in the select from String command, which is accessible through the select menu.

title: Session files
text:
PMV 1.5.6 introduces a new session file. It no longer relies on log strings and on playing back the entire session, which was error prone and slow.
The new session file is self-contained: you can send it to another user and it restores the session. It contains a Python script that issues all the PMV commands needed to create the molecular geometries and configure them as they were when the session was saved. Vision networks are saved and restored too.
Session files are gzipped tar files with the extension .psf (PMV Session File).






NoteLimitations




Molecules read from PDBQ, PDBQT and PDBQS files are saved in their original format. All other molecules are currently saved as PDB files, which can lose information (for example from mol2 files).
Only ATOM, HETATM and CONECT records are saved for molecules in a session file. For example, a molecule read from a PDB file with secondary structure records loses these records when restored from a session, so its secondary structure is assigned programmatically and may differ from the PDB records.
Some representations are not restored: splines, CA traces, distance, angle and torsion measurements, and isosurfaces of volumetric data.
Geometry not created by PMV (for example created in Vision) is not restored.

title: Release notes
text:
New in MGLTools 1.5.6:

New Panel for holding interfaces for a variety of tools.
Redesigned Dashboard widget with enhanced functionality.
New functionality for creating 3D animations.
New widget panel for measuring tools and for altering 3D rendering attributes of molecular geometrical objects.
New ribbon representation called Beaded Ribbons.
New GPU-based Screen Space Ambient Occlusion rendering mode (press the “O” key on the keyboard while the mouse pointer is in the 3D view).
Redesigned color chooser widget.
Faster and more robust mechanism for saving and restoring sessions which no longer relies on using log strings.
New shortcuts for selecting Water, Ions, DNA, RNA, Amino Acids and Ligands (see Selection command menu in Dashboard widget.).
Added the ability to grow the current selection by extending the selection to close by atoms, as well as selecting atoms in the neighborhood of the current selection (select around). These function are available through the new Dashboard widget.
Flashing geometry are used to identify molecular fragments for picking operations.
Cursors indicate the type of operation the mouse is performing (e.g. rotation, translation, selection, etc.)
Rotation has been moved from middle mouse button to left mouse button.
Shift Left button adds to the current selection, Control Left button removes from the current selection.
Lazy evaluation of log strings. The creation of log strings can slow down operation and sometimes very large lists of strings have to be created. starting with 1.5.6, Pmv only generates the log strings when the text port showing log strings is visible.
Proper handling of MODRES records. The PDB parsers now properly handle MODRES records used to specify modified amino acids. This allows secondary structure to not be interrupted anymore by such residues and the selecting of amino acids to properly include such residues.
New command for generating bibliographic information for images created with Pmv. This command is available under the Help menu and allows listing the subset of references needed based on the types of representations visible in the scene ( Help → Cite This Scene ).
New commands were added under the Display menu for labeling atoms, residues, chains and molecules (Display → Label → Atoms, Residues, Chains and Molecules).
A new user preference called PDB Cache Storage is now used to control maximum space allowed for File → Read → fetch From Web. When the size of cached files exceeds the preference value, the oldest files are deleted from the cache.
In 3D Grid changed Volume Rendering widget to include “Use This Widget” and “Use Colormap GUI” options. Fixed “Set Color” menu in Transfer Function editor; this menu is now always on and it updates colors properly.
Added Color → Rainbow that colors molecules using a rainbow color map.
Added new user preference that allows users to choose geometry used for selection. Possible values are none, spheres, crosses. If set to none, no changes are visible in the viewer when doing selection.
The Compute → Molecular Surface command was redesigned. The perMol check button and surface name entry was removed. The command when invoked from the menu now always computes a surface for the whole molecule and names it MSMS-MOL. A check button was added to allow excluding Hetero atoms from the surface calculation. This is useful for instance when water molecules are present but should be ignored when computing the surface. This button is unchecked in order to be backwards compatible.
Redesigned color palette widget.
Updated AutoLigand and its GUI to include two new modes of running. Users can now run AutoLigand in Connected Fill or Scan mode. Connected Fill allows to constrain the start and end location for the fill. Users can change xyz coordinates for the start and end location represented in the GUI as yellow and cyan crosses, respectively. This information is then passed to AutoLigand which tries to fill the grid with atoms that start at the start location and end at the end location. In the Scan mode, AutoLigand scans the whole grid and tries to find the best fill with a given number of points regardless of a starting position. This was previously done with separate scripts.
Added a citation entry for AutoLigand:
self.vf.showCitation.citations["AutoLigand"] = """Please acknowledge the use of the AutoLigand that results in any published work, including scientific papers, films and videotapes, by citing the following reference: Harris R, Olson AJ, Goodsell DS.  Proteins. (2008) 70 1506.."""

title: Camera tools
text:
The Camera Tools group controls common attributes of the 3D Viewer rendering window (the camera).
Background and fog. Set the background color with the color wheel button . Depth cueing mixes the background color into the color of displayed objects according to their distance from the viewer; this fog-like effect enhances 3D perception. By default the fog color is the same as the background color. Clicking the chain icon  between the two color wheel buttons stops the fog color from following the background. Once the link is broken , the second color wheel button becomes enabled and sets a fog color different from the background color. The picture below shows a white background with black fog.

Anti-aliasing. The AA button  sets the level of anti-aliasing. Anti-aliasing smooths the edges of lines and polygons by redrawing the scene several times while jittering the camera and accumulating pixel values. The higher the AA number, the smoother the edges; but since it is the number of times the scene is drawn, rendering can slow down. Modern graphics cards usually support 4×AA in hardware with no noticeable performance penalty.
Clipping and fog range. The clipZ thumbwheels  set the near and far clipping planes, which define the start and end of the 3D scene along the viewing axis. The fog thumbwheels  set where the depth-cueing fog begins and ends, unless the fog is tied to the Z clipping planes; then it follows the near and far planes automatically. The vertical chain button  to the right of the thumbwheels ties the fog to the Z clipping planes.

title: AutoDock CrankPep (ADCP)
text:
AutoDock CrankPep (ADCP) is a docking engine specialized for peptides. It combines a protein folding technique with AutoDock’s efficient representation of a rigid receptor as affinity grids. A Monte Carlo search folds the peptide while it optimizes the peptide’s interaction with the receptor, which yields docked peptides. ADCP takes a peptide as a sequence string and has docked peptides of up to 20 amino acids successfully.
ADCP is part of the AutoDock Suite.

title: AutoDock CrankPep (ADCP)
text:
What changed in version 1.1
Version 1.1 adds support for non-standard amino acids and lets you minimize docked poses with OpenMM. In detail:

Streamlined output. Docked poses are saved in a single multi-model PDB file, xxx_out.pdb, where xxx is the job name (or a default name), and a summary file xxx_summary.dlg is written.
Full side chains. Docked poses contain all-atom side chains instead of a rotamer index.
Number of poses. Set how many docked poses to write with -m / --nmodes.
Command line changes. The target file is given with -T and can be a .trg file or a folder containing one. The new option -k keeps calculation details.
Rotamer libraries. Side-chain rotamers are loaded from .lib text files; system rotamer libraries are selected with -L.
Non-standard amino acids. Rotamers for modified side chains can be added without recompiling. The syntax <FOO> names the side chain used for the full-atom representation, preceded by the letter of the coarse potential.
D-amino acids. Write & before the coarse potential letter.
Histidine protonation states. HIE and HID are supported.
Automatic affinity maps. ADCP loads affinity maps for every atom type detected in the peptide.
MD refinement. Docked poses can be minimized with OpenMM, with options to control it.

title: ADCP 1.0 documentation
text:
FAQ

How many steps and replicas are enough for my peptide?

The longer the peptide, the harder the docking problem, so run more replicas with more steps if resources allow. As a guideline, run 100–300 replicas with a maximum of 1–3 million Monte Carlo steps per amino acid (10–30 million steps for a 10-mer).

Should I start from a helix, an extended structure, or a mixture?

If you know something about the peptide’s conformation, start from that conformation. Starting from one conformation does not prevent sampling of others with different secondary structure. If nothing is known, start from a mixture of 80% extended and 20% helical conformations.

Why are there clashes in the output structure?

ADCP builds side chains from a discrete rotamer library and uses a coarse-grained scoring function for the internal energy. The output can therefore have minor clashes and non-ideal bond angles and lengths. Minimize the structure with any molecular mechanics force field to fix them. (Version 1.1 adds OpenMM minimization.)

Where are the caps at the peptide termini?

Peptide termini come in different types, and adding the proper caps did not conclusively help docking. ADCP therefore docks without caps. You can add caps to the output structure with software such as VMD or PyMOL.

How to create a PDBQT file for a rigid receptor
This creates a PDBQT file for a rigid receptor from a PDB file. The PDBQT file can be used as input for AGFR, ADFR and ADCP, and for AutoDock4 and AutoDock Vina.
For docking ligands it is usually better to use the biologically active molecule (the biological assembly), which is sometimes different from the asymmetric unit in a PDB file. For this example we searched the PDB for 4EK3 and downloaded the biological assembly, saved as 4ek3.pdb1 in our download folder.
Next, add hydrogen atoms. prepare_receptor can add hydrogens with OpenBabel, but we found that reduce from the Richardson lab tends to give better results. reduce is included in ADFRsuite. Run it from the command line:

On Windows, the ADFRSuite/bin folder is added to the path automatically, so you can type reduce directly in a Windows command prompt (Start menu, type cmd).


Then generate the PDBQT file with prepare_receptor:
$ADFRsuite_INSTALL_DIR/bin/prepare_receptor -r 4ek3H.pdb -o 4ek3.pdbqt

text: Here we assume that you already created or loaded a target file, else the button for inspecting/visualizing maps will be disabled.

title: Tutorial: visualizing affinity maps
text:
1. Map viz. widget
Click  to display the map visualization GUI
The graphical user interface for visualizing maps presents a list of target files that can be expanded to show affinity maps. By default, only the carbon (C), Oxygen (OA), and hydrogen (HD) maps are listed.

title: Tutorial: visualizing affinity maps
text:
2. Nitrogen map
Right click on the target file name in the widget to add the nitrogen map

title: Tutorial: visualizing affinity maps
text:
3. Isocontour
Right-click on the nitrogen map and select “add isocontour”
The isocontour is displayed in blue in the 3D viewer. A widget allowing to customize the isocontour is displayed in the GUI. The isocontour level can be modified by dragging the red cursor over the histogram.


Notes:

The range of values for which the histogram is display can be customized using the typein widgets below the histogram.
The 2 bars of widgets below the histogram control the rendering of the front ‘f’ and back ‘b’ facing polygons of the isocontour mesh. The options are to render the mesh as dots only, a set of lines outlining the triangles in the mesh, a shaded surface, or a shaded surface with a mesh on top. The last button in the bar opens a color picker to define the isocontour color. (you might have to resize the widget horizontally to reveal the button).
Right clicking on some of these widgets displays an options menu.

title: Tutorial: visualizing affinity maps
text:
4. Orthoslice
Right-click on the nitrogen map and select “add orthoslice ->Z”
The orthoslice is display using the default color map. A color map editor widget is displayed in the GUI allowing to interactively modify the hue, saturation, luminosity and opacity of the transfer function. The range of values mapped to colors is displayed below the color map editor along with a slider for moving the slice through the volume.

Notes:

Color maps can be saved to and loaded from files through the File menu
The number of color entries in the color map can be set under the Edit menu
Modifications of the color map channels support unlimited undo/redo (CtrlZ/Ctrl R)
A set of pre-defined maps are available under the Maps menu.
The 4 channels of the map (hue, saturation, luminosity and opacity) can be changed interactively using the mouse. Shift-Click and drag allows drawing a line to define a linear ramp.
HSVA channels: think of Hue as the color shade, Saturation as the amount of black you mix in the color, Luminosity is how much white you mix in the color, and Opacity is how opaque the color is (1.0: completely opaque, 0.0 totally transparent).

title: Tutorial: docking box from an AutoSite pocket
text:
In this scenario we have a receptor but no ligand binding site information. We use AutoSite to identify possible binding pockets that we use to define the docking box and calculate maps.
We will illustrate this use case with cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2, PDB 4EK3). The receptor file 4EK3_rec.pdbqt is available in the tutorial data file.
Start the graphical interface with ADFRsuite-1.0/bin/agfrgui.

title: Tutorial: docking box from an AutoSite pocket
text:
1. Load receptor
Click  and select 4EK3_rec.pdbqt
The receptor molecule is loaded and displayed as lines representing atomic bonds colored by atom type with carbon atoms shown in cyan. The default docking-box covers the entire receptor with the default padding (4.0 Angstroms) added to each side.

Notes:

Amino acids located in the docking box with no flexible side-chains (i.e. glycine, alanine and proline) are displayed with dimmed down lines.
Several buttons in the control section and the tool-bar are now enabled.
The status bar indicates that the next step could be to detect pockets.

The 3D scene can be rotated, translated and scaled using the 3 mouse buttons:



Mouse button

Left
